analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal anti-harassment and discrimination law and phases out the lower tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on February 12, 2026 with 20 Democratic and independent cosponsors, and referred to the Senate HELP committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make several major changes to workplace civil rights law. It would require employers with 15 or more workers to adopt and enforce anti-harassment policies and training, extend discrimination protections down to one-employee businesses and to contractors, interns, and volunteers, remove the caps on damages victims can win, make a single incident of harassment actionable, and bar employers from forcing discrimination claims into secret arbitration. It would also phase out the two-tier 'tipped minimum wage' over several years so tipped workers must be paid the full federal minimum wage in cash, and would fund legal help for low-income workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination, especially low-wage and tipped workers who currently must prove 'severe or pervasive' conduct and can be forced into arbitration; tipped workers, whose required cash wage would rise from $2.13 toward the full federal minimum; small-business employees, since coverage would drop from 15 employees to 1; contractors, interns, and volunteers, who are currently unprotected; LGBTQ workers, whose protection from sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination would be written into statute; and low-income workers, who would get grant-funded legal assistance.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out the tipped minimum wage: the required cash wage for tipped employees rises to $3.60 an hour on enactment, then climbs each year (up to $1.50 per year) until it equals the full federal minimum wage, and employers are barred from keeping any portion of employees' tips.

Requires every employer with 15 or more employees to adopt, post, and annually disseminate a comprehensive nondiscrimination policy, with multiple reporting channels and anti-retaliation protections, and fines employers $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for repeated or willful violations) for noncompliance; the EEOC would also set interactive training requirements for employees and supervisors.

Writes into Title VII that discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, and pregnancy is unlawful sex discrimination, and states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a claim or defense against Title VII claims.

Makes workplace harassment itself a statutory violation under Title VII and parallel laws covering age, disability, and genetic information, with a totality-of-the-circumstances standard under which a single incident can be enough, and conduct no longer must be 'severe or pervasive' as a threshold.

Expands who is covered: the definition of 'employer' drops from 15 employees to 1, and protections extend to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees; statutes of limitations for filing claims would be extended, and caps on compensatory and punitive damages would be removed.

The table of contents includes sections restricting nondisclosure agreements (Sec. 302) and prohibiting mandatory arbitration while protecting concerted legal action (Sec. 303), so discrimination claims could not be forced into private arbitration and silenced through NDAs as a condition of employment.

Creates grant programs for legal assistance to low-income workers on employment discrimination claims and for a national system of state worker advocacy, plus a national Census-run prevalence survey on workplace harassment every three years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers. Restaurants and other tipped-service businesses would face substantially higher wage bills as the tip credit phases out and could no longer count customers' tips toward wages. All covered employers would bear policy, training, and compliance costs; would lose forced arbitration and broad NDAs as tools; would face uncapped compensatory and punitive damages; and smaller businesses would newly be covered at the one-employee threshold.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is mandatory and penalized: employers that fail to adopt or post the required policy face fines of up to $1,000 per violation, rising to at least $5,000 per violation if repeated or willful, a real cost for small firms with thin margins.

Removing the caps on compensatory and punitive damages and lowering the harassment bar to allow single-incident claims would increase litigation exposure and settlement costs across employers, which critics of similar measures argue will be passed to consumers or priced into fewer hours and jobs.

Phasing out the tip credit imposes a large, abrupt cost shift on full-service restaurants, whose operators have historically argued that eliminating the tipped minimum wage can reduce flexible tipped jobs and pressure small independent restaurants hardest; the bill's gradual $1.50-per-year step-up is designed to soften but not eliminate that shock.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for workers are large and concrete: a full cash minimum wage for tipped workers, protection down to one-employee firms, legal representation funded for low-income workers, and an end to forced arbitration of discrimination claims. The honest costs are higher wage bills for restaurants, compliance costs and fines for small employers, and broader litigation risk from uncapped damages and a lowered harassment threshold. The bill is clearly designed to shift bargaining power toward workers; whether the wage and litigation costs land mainly on employers or partly on consumers and hours is the real empirical dispute.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on day one, and it has sat there since with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, joined by 20 cosponsors — 19 Democrats and 1 independent.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Since referral, the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers and businesses that rely on the tipped minimum wage are better off: the current lower wage floor, damages caps, forced arbitration, and NDA practices all remain untouched, and the bill's backers are still waiting for any committee action at all.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the initial cosponsor list.

for.name: 20 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 19 Democrats and 1 independent, including Sens. Baldwin, Booker, Sanders, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate calendar and committee leadership
against.what_they_did: No member of the majority cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the cross-party support historically needed to move a labor bill to the floor.

against.name: Restaurant industry associations
against.what_they_did: Have historically campaigned against eliminating the tip credit in prior Congresses, the same provision this bill contains; no opposition activity appears in the congressional record for this bill yet.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 21 sponsors and cosponsors is a Democrat or independent; no Republican has signed on, and the Senate is under Republican control.

industries.note: The bill phases out the tip credit, requiring tipped workers' cash wage to climb to the full federal minimum within a few years and barring employers from keeping any tips. That transfers wage costs back onto employers from customers' tips, which is why the industry has historically fought this change hardest.

industries.industry: Large employers and the workplace arbitration industry
industries.note: The bill bans mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims (Sec. 303), restricts NDAs (Sec. 302), removes damages caps, extends statutes of limitations, and drops coverage down to one-employee firms — dismantling the current structure under which most discrimination claims are resolved privately and confidentially.

They would newly be covered by federal discrimination law at the one-employee threshold, a new compliance and liability cost; however, the EEOC would provide them free model policies and trainings designed for their resources, so they gain protections for workers they may employ at real cost to owners.

industries.industry: Worker legal aid and employment plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: Grant programs for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and a national system of state worker advocacy would directly fund lawyers and advocates, while longer filing windows and an easier harassment standard increase the viable caseload.

analysis.trajectory: Versions of the BE HEARD Act have been reintroduced in several Congresses without ever advancing past committee referral. With no Republican cosponsors, a Republican Senate majority, and no committee action since introduction, the realistic path this Congress is that it sits in committee without a hearing or vote unless the chamber's control changes.
